Hirschprung's disease is a disorder where nerve cells do not migrate normally during embryonic development, resulting in an aganglionic segment of bowel.  This causes an inability of the smooth muscles in the bowel wall to relax, which results in a blockage that prevents food from passing through the intestines. This condition most commonly affects males under age 20, but it can occur at any age. Symptoms include diarrhoea, vomiting and swelling in the abdomen, as well as poor appetite and weight loss. Hirschsprung's disease usually affects only one section of the large intestine (colon). Children who are born prematurely or who have Down syndrome may be more likely to develop this condition. The cause of Hirschsprung's disease isn't clear. It may result from a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Treatment often involves surgery to remove the affected section of the colon. Dietary changes and medications also may help control symptoms. Dendritic cells are located at the front line of defence (skin), whereas macrophages are found in peripheral tissues and the bloodstream. Both possess PRRs which bind to PAMPs (Pathogen-Associated Molecular Patterns) on the pathogen's surface. This triggers a release of inflammatory cytokines. Dendritic cells migrate to nearest draining lymph node where they interact with naive T cells. They present MHC/peptide complexes to these T cells, activating them into effector T cells. Macrophages cannot migrate to the nearest draining lymph node. They cannot activate naive T cells directly as they lack co-stimulatory molecules required for activation. They can however perform phagocytosis - engulfing and lysing pathogens. Effector T cells then trigger the adaptive immune response. All cells of the innate immune system express Class I MHC receptors. Class I MHC receptors display peptides derived from intracellular microbes to CD8+ T cells. These T cells kill infected cells. X = AdenosineY = DaylightZ = ATP Stores Caffeine competitively antagonises adenosine receptors. Adenosine is produced by Guanosine and increases when ATP levels decrease. It promotes sleep by inducing vasodilation (causing sleep as core body temperature decreases) as well as increasing the release of serotonin which also causes sleep. If you reduce the amount of adenosine by consuming large amounts of caffeine, you will feel less tired.  During daytime, adenosine levels are low due to high amounts of daylight which inhibits its production. This is why we don't want to consume caffeine in the day! When night falls, adenosine levels increase as there is no daylight inhibition. We then store up ATP so that we have energy during the night and can get to sleep. This is done by converting ADP into ATP. ATP is stored in muscles as creatine phosphate or glycogen and in the liver as glucose. If you do not store your ATP, adenosine will continue to promote sleep. Therefore, if you are awake at night, you need to make sure you store your ATP. If you are feeling tired during the day, this means that you haven't stored enough ATP and you should go to bed early to ensure that you do.  The reason why caffeine makes you more awake is because it prevents your body from storing ATP. By preventing ATP storage, you are unable to convert adenosine into adenine and therefore cannot get to sleep. This is why you feel awake when consuming caffeine. Hyper/hypoventilation is defined by the ratio between alveolar ventilation (VA) and CO2 production (VCO2). If VA > VCO2 then there is hyperventilation and if VA < VCO2 then there is hypoventilation. Disease states with increased physiological dead space is an example of why there would be hypoventilation.  'Physiological Dead Space' is the volume of air inspired into the lung that does not participate in gas exchange because it is not perfused by the pulmonary capillary bed. It consists of the volume of air contained in the conducting zone of the lung and the volume of air that does not reach the periphery of the lung because of its movement away from the blood vessels towards the bronchial tree.  When there is a disease state with increased physiological dead space there is hypoventilation. This is because the lungs are less well ventilated so there is higher arterial PCO2 and lower arterial pO2.  In health there is a balance between the respiratory muscles and the chemoreceptors. If the respiratory system detects a rise in PCO2 then there will be an increase in ventilation to remove the excess carbon dioxide. However, in conditions with increased physiological dead space there is hypoventilation. B is the correct answer as arteriosclerosis describes the hardening and thickening of the arteries whereas atherosclerosis involves the formation of an atheroma which is a plaque made up of LDLs, other substances such as cholesterol and white blood cells that have entered the sub-endothelium and collagen fibres fused together by foam cells. This process of fatty deposits forming on the walls of arteries is called atherogenesis and it occurs when the endothelium becomes damaged - this damage may be caused by smoking, high cholesterol diet or high blood pressure. The damaged endothelium allows LDLs to enter into the sub-endothelium where they are then engulfed by macrophages. The macrophage is now known as a foam cell because it has engulfed so much fat. As more macrophages are attracted to the area, the fatty deposit grows larger until it becomes an atheroma. When blood passes through the artery, the atheroma may protrude into the lumen and cause turbulent flow of the blood. The atheroma may also rupture causing a clot to form which blocks the blood supply completely. NSAIDs inhibit PGI2 production from the endothelium and so the balance in arteries favours TXA2, a vasoconstrictor, and thus promotes the likelihood of thrombosis through vasoconstriction of vascular smooth muscle cells and platelet aggregation.  NSAIDs are non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs which work by competitive inhibition of the COX domain enzyme (prostaglandin H synthase) which produces prostaglandins and thromboxane. Thromboxane is produced from the same enzyme but acts on platelets to promote aggregation and vasoconstriction of vascular smooth muscle cells. Therefore inhibiting PGE2 and PGI2 production will result in less competition for the thromboxane pathway and favour a pro-thrombotic environment.
